paragraphs: This paper learns to predict average human ratings of facial attractiveness from images. The training information combines measurements of facial geometry, color, and texture with an average attractiveness score for each face. Several predictors are trained, and the final predictor produces ratings that are highly correlated with human judgments, substantially improving on earlier machine learning results described in the abstract.

The authors also examine what the predictor has learned by testing it on virtually altered facial images. These simulated psychophysical experiments ask how its judgments change when the appearance of a face changes. The resulting preferences resemble human preferences, connecting the predictor's behavior to hypotheses about facial averageness, smoothness, and symmetry.

The central finding goes beyond agreement on numerical ratings. A system trained specifically to match attractiveness scores also develops judgment patterns resembling human perceptual biases. This makes the predictor useful for investigating those biases, while its target remains the human ratings used for learning rather than an independent definition of attractiveness.
neurips-2006-a-humanlike-predictor-of-fa.tldr: A predictor trained on facial features and human attractiveness ratings also develops preferences resembling human perceptual biases.

paragraphs: This paper studies how local image information attracts human eye movements. Many computational saliency models begin with filters chosen to resemble biological visual processing, then combine their outputs into an attention score. That design requires decisions about filter types, sizes, weights, and nonlinear transformations, some of which lack a clear biological justification.

The authors instead learn a saliency model directly from human eye movement data. Their approach is deliberately simple and described as essentially parameter-free. The aim is to let the relationship between images and observed gaze guide the model, reducing reliance on the many manually chosen components used by existing approaches.

Experiments show performance comparable to existing models despite the absence of built-in biological knowledge. The learned features also resemble earlier findings about vision: patterns that most strongly activate the model have a center-surround organization similar to early visual receptive fields. The result shows that such structure can emerge from learning to predict eye movements, without being explicitly supplied as a prior.
neurips-2006-a-nonparametric-approach-to.tldr: A simple saliency model learned from eye movements matches existing approaches and develops features resembling early visual receptive fields.

paragraphs: This paper applies reinforcement learning and optimal control to autonomous aerobatic helicopter flight. It reports the first successful autonomous completion on a real radio-controlled helicopter of four maneuvers: a low-speed forward flip, a low-speed sideways roll, a tail-in funnel, and a nose-in funnel. These demonstrations address a control problem that the authors describe as highly challenging.

The approach begins with a human pilot flying the helicopter. Those flights help the researchers identify a model of helicopter dynamics and a reward, or cost, function. Together, these specify how the modeled helicopter responds and what the controller should optimize. A learning algorithm then finds a controller optimized for that model and objective.

The specific algorithm is differential dynamic programming, an extension of the linear quadratic regulator. The contribution connects pilot-informed modeling with controller optimization and physical flight demonstrations. The reported advance is therefore grounded in successful maneuvers on an actual helicopter, with the learned controller tied to the dynamics model and reward function developed from the pilot's flights.
neurips-2006-an-application-of-reinforce.tldr: Pilot-informed dynamics modeling and differential dynamic programming enable a real helicopter to autonomously perform four aerobatic maneuvers.

paragraphs: This paper addresses locating and separating several sound sources in a stereo recording. Its method is designed to remain robust when reverberation is present, and it does not require assumptions about the statistical behavior of the sources. That makes the recording model, rather than a prescribed source distribution, central to the approach.

The authors construct a probabilistic model of recordings containing multiple sources across two channels. They fit it using expectation maximization to find maximum-likelihood parameters. These parameters include distributions over delays and assignments of regions in time and frequency to particular sources. The assignments connect portions of the observed recording to the sources the system is trying to distinguish.

Evaluation uses simulated simultaneous speech from two or three sources and compares the method with two comparable algorithms. It performs better than both in conditions without reverberation. With reverberation, it matches the better competing method. The findings therefore support both source separation and localization through probabilistic fitting, with different comparative outcomes depending on the acoustic conditions.
neurips-2006-an-em-algorithm-for-localiz.tldr: A probabilistic stereo model localizes and separates sound sources, outperforming two alternatives without reverberation and matching the better one with reverberation.

paragraphs: Inference in graphical models often requires quantities that are difficult to compute when the graph contains cycles. Many approximation methods use tractable tree models as building blocks. This paper explores a different building block: planar graphs, which can retain cycles while still supporting exact calculations under particular restrictions.

The tractable models have binary variables and interaction potentials without an external field. For this restricted class, an existing exact algorithm computes the partition function, the quantity that normalizes the model's probabilities. The authors use these planar models in a decomposition that produces upper bounds on the partition function of non-planar models. Their algorithm also estimates marginal probabilities for individual variables and pairs.

Compared with the tree decomposition method identified in the abstract, the planar decomposition gives a much tighter partition-function bound and better pairwise marginals, while singleton marginals are comparable. The findings distinguish improvements in joint relationships from estimates for individual variables. They show the value of using richer tractable components for approximation, within the stated restrictions on those components.
neurips-2006-approximate-inference-using.tldr: Decomposing graphical models into tractable planar components yields tighter partition-function bounds and better pairwise marginals than the compared tree decomposition.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning when only a small portion of the available features matters. Its initial target is a decision list of length k over n Boolean variables. The question is whether learning can require relatively few examples even when the full set of variables contains many irrelevant features.

The authors show that smooth boosting methods, including MadaBoost, can efficiently learn these lists with an example count polynomial in k and log n. The guarantee is conditional: the distribution over the relevant variables must not be too concentrated, measured in an L2-norm sense. Under that condition, the dependence on the total number of variables is through its logarithm rather than directly through n.

The analysis also extends to linear threshold functions with k nonzero coefficients, yielding a similar but quantitatively weaker result. Experiments indicate that using smooth boosting affects actual algorithm performance as well as enabling the theoretical analysis. The contribution thus links a distributional condition and a particular boosting approach to learning efficiently amid many irrelevant attributes.
neurips-2006-attribute-efficient-learnin.tldr: Smooth boosting learns short decision lists from few examples under an unconcentrated-distribution condition, with a weaker extension to sparse linear threshold functions.

paragraphs: This paper studies decisions about whether to continue processing an item through a sequence of stages. Continuing consumes time and resources but may also produce additional value. The learning problem is to decide when that extra processing is worthwhile, using only the information available at the current stage.

The proposed framework learns a separate decision rule for each stage from historical data. Together, those rules determine how far an item proceeds through the pipeline. This connects learning to the structure of a processing sequence: later decisions can use information accumulated along the way, while earlier decisions must act before that information has been gathered.

The authors show how the framework covers settings ranging from manufacturing to vision processing, and they provide empirical results for object detection. They also derive a testing-performance bound with quadratic dependence on the number of decisions. This supplies a theoretical account of how the length of the decision sequence enters the bound, alongside an application demonstrating the framework in visual processing.
neurips-2006-chained-boosting-af80d0155e.tldr: Chained boosting learns stage-specific rules for deciding whether the potential value of further processing justifies its cost.

paragraphs: This paper presents a shared computational method for comparing sequential data. It covers several kinds of comparison: kernel functions, distances, and similarities that do not satisfy metric requirements. The aim is to support this range of measures through one generic algorithm rather than treating each type as an unrelated computational problem.

The algorithm uses generalized suffix trees to calculate the comparisons efficiently. Its stated worst-case running time is linear in sequence length and does not depend on the underlying embedding language. That language specifies the sequence elements being represented, which may include words, fixed-length k-grams, or all contained subsequences. The result connects a broad choice of representations with the same stated runtime behavior.

Experiments span network intrusion detection, DNA analysis, and text processing. They demonstrate the usefulness of sequence distances and similarity coefficients as alternatives to classical kernels. The contribution combines computational efficiency with flexibility in how sequences are compared, making the choice of similarity measure part of the modeling approach rather than restricting it to kernels alone.
neurips-2006-computation-of-similarity-m.tldr: A generalized-suffix-tree algorithm computes diverse sequence similarities with worst-case runtime linear in sequence length.

paragraphs: People's category decisions depend on the examples they have recently encountered. After seeing an example of one category, that category's apparent prototype shifts toward the example, while other category prototypes shift away. These effects weaken with experience and likely reflect longer-term learning of category boundaries. This paper evaluates four probabilistic explanations of those patterns.

All four models describe examples within a category using a Gaussian distribution in feature space. To categorize an example, they calculate probabilities for the possible categories. They differ along two dimensions: whether uncertainty about category prototypes has a localist or distributed representation, and whether learning uses maximum-likelihood gradient ascent or a Kalman filter update.

The distributed maximum-likelihood model explains the central experimental phenomena. It also predicts additional effects that are confirmed by reanalyzing the experimental data. The result supports that particular combination of representation and learning rule as an account of the observed context effects. Its contribution includes explaining known behavior and generating further predictions that the existing data support.
neurips-2006-context-effects-in-category.tldr: Among four probabilistic models, a distributed maximum-likelihood model explains category context effects and predicts additional patterns confirmed in reanalyzed data.

paragraphs: This paper considers sample selection bias, where training data and test data come from different distributions. The training sample therefore represents a different mix of inputs from the one encountered at test time. Correcting that mismatch requires deciding how the training observations should contribute when learning for the test distribution.

The proposed nonparametric method directly computes resampling weights. It does so by matching the training and test distributions in feature space, using unlabeled data to inform the correction. This differs from approaches that first estimate the sampling distributions and then derive weights from those estimates. Here, the desired correction is obtained without that intermediate distribution-estimation step.

The authors report experimental evidence that the method works well in practice. The main methodological contribution is the direct route from a distribution mismatch to weights that adjust the training sample's representation. Feature-space matching supplies the criterion for those weights, connecting information about the test inputs to the treatment of training examples without requiring labels for the test data.
neurips-2006-correcting-sample-selection.tldr: A nonparametric method corrects sample selection bias by directly learning resampling weights through feature-space distribution matching.

paragraphs: This paper learns how to measure visual similarity for image retrieval and classification. Its central choice is to learn a local distance function for each training image. Similarity is therefore adapted around individual training examples, giving each image its own learned way of comparing visual content.

Each local function combines elementary distances between visual features extracted from image patches. These combined functions are then used to retrieve images and classify previously unseen ones. The approach places the learning effort in the comparison rule: patch-based measurements provide the ingredients, and their learned combination determines the distance associated with a training image.

On the Caltech 101 object recognition benchmark, the method achieves 60.3% mean recognition across classes with 15 training images per class. The authors report that this exceeds the best previously published result they compare against. That finding supports the usefulness of learning image-specific combinations of feature distances for recognition. The stated numerical result concerns classification, while the framework is also applied to image retrieval.
neurips-2006-image-retrieval-and-classif.tldr: Learning a separate patch-feature distance function for each training image achieves 60.3% mean recognition on Caltech 101 with 15 examples per class.

paragraphs: This paper introduces two algorithms for online learning in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. In this setting, a predictor is updated as observations arrive, and kernels provide the space in which learning takes place. The first algorithm, ILK, centers on a new implicit update technique that applies to a wide variety of convex loss functions.

The second algorithm, SILK, is a sparse version of ILK designed to use bounded memory. It maintains a compact predictor representation while preserving solution quality, including in non-stationary environments where the learning setting changes over time. This addresses the representation of the predictor alongside the rule used to update it.

The authors establish loss bounds and analyze convergence rates for both methods. They also report experiments on synthetic and real data in which the proposed algorithms outperform the methods used for comparison. The contribution combines a broadly applicable update mechanism, a bounded-memory variant, and theoretical analysis, with empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of both approaches in the tested settings.
neurips-2006-implicit-online-learning-wi.tldr: ILK introduces implicit kernel-learning updates, while SILK provides a bounded-memory version with theoretical guarantees and favorable experimental results.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to train discriminative random fields using both labeled and unlabeled data. The goal is to improve image-processing models that capture spatial dependencies. Its semi-supervised formulation allows images without supplied labels to influence training alongside examples whose desired outputs are known.

Training is expressed as maximum a posteriori estimation. The objective combines conditional log-likelihood on labeled data, a data-dependent prior, and a conditional entropy regularizer on unlabeled data. These terms bring supervised evidence and unlabeled examples into a single optimization problem. The resulting objective is no longer concave, so the authors develop an efficient local optimization procedure.

The method is applied to segmentation on synthetic and real datasets. In each case, the authors report significant improvements over supervised discriminative random fields. These findings support the practical benefit of incorporating unlabeled information into training for the tested tasks. The optimization result is a workable local procedure for the new objective, paired with evidence of more accurate classifiers than standard supervised training produces.
neurips-2006-learning-to-model-spatial-d.tldr: A semi-supervised training objective for discriminative random fields uses unlabeled data to improve segmentation on synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: This paper addresses estimating the pose of articulated objects from a single static image. Such objects have many independently varying parts, creating many quantities to estimate. The authors follow a probabilistic approach to pose inference, while emphasizing that the quality of visual features often strongly influences how well these methods work.

Their main contribution is to treat inference as an iterative parsing process. As the process proceeds, it learns increasingly effective features tailored to the particular image being analyzed. Feature learning thus becomes part of interpreting the image, allowing the representation used for inference to improve over successive steps.

Quantitative experiments on a database of more than 300 human images suggest performance competitive with, or better than, the state of the art. The procedure does not depend on detecting faces or skin, and the authors also apply it to horse pose estimation in the Weizmann database. Together, these applications show how the image-specific parsing approach can extend beyond human bodies.
neurips-2006-learning-to-parse-images-of.tldr: An iterative parsing method learns features tailored to each image to estimate human and horse poses.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to remove noise from points sampled around an unknown submanifold in a higher-dimensional space. The underlying geometric structure is not supplied to the algorithm. It must work from the noisy points themselves, so denoising and the geometry of the sample are closely connected.

The proposed method uses a graph-based diffusion process on the point sample. The graph provides the structure through which the diffusion acts on the data. The authors analyze that process using results about convergence of graph Laplacians, connecting the graph operation to the geometric setting in which the points were sampled.

Experiments show that the method can handle nontrivial noise in high-dimensional data. The authors also use it as preprocessing for a semi-supervised learning algorithm and obtain improved results. This second finding gives the denoising operation a downstream role: cleaning the sample can help a subsequent learner. Both results support the usefulness of diffusion-based denoising when the underlying manifold must be inferred from noisy observations.
neurips-2006-manifold-denoising-4e6fef4b.tldr: Graph-based diffusion denoises samples from an unknown manifold and improves a semi-supervised learner when used as preprocessing.

paragraphs: This paper examines regression when training inputs and test inputs follow different distributions, a situation described as covariate shift. It develops a Bayesian generative perspective on the problem. The aim is to account for the distribution mismatch within the regression model rather than treating the mismatch as separate from prediction.

The authors show that earlier approaches to covariate shift can be understood through mixture regression. That view leads to a general procedure combining regression and density estimation. Training and test densities therefore do not have to be supplied as known quantities; estimating them is incorporated into the same procedure that learns the regression relationship.

Previous methods emerge as special cases of the formulation. This unification matters because it makes their implicit assumptions easier to understand and places them within a broader modeling framework. The paper's stated contribution is a general way to organize regression under distribution shift, with joint estimation replacing the need to begin from already-known input densities.
neurips-2006-mixture-regression-for-cova.tldr: A Bayesian mixture-regression framework jointly estimates densities and regression under covariate shift, recovering earlier methods as special cases.

paragraphs: This paper connects a model of viral evolution with prediction of HIV drug resistance from genotype. Its starting point is the generative-discriminative approach: a generative model describes domain structure, and a kernel converts that structure into a similarity measure for a statistical learner. The authors focus on making that model specific to the biological mechanism.

Their MTreeMix kernel measures similarity between viral sequence samples in terms of evolutionary escape from antiviral drug pressure. This supplies a biologically informed comparison for support vector regression. The authors compare it with a standard amino acid encoding that does not incorporate evolutionary information.

Across 17 anti-HIV drugs, the study reports significant improvements in predictive performance with the new kernel. The finding supports using a model of the relevant evolutionary process to inform genotype-based resistance prediction. In this study, the kernel provides the connection between population genetic modeling and a prediction task relevant to clinical decisions, showing how domain-specific generative structure can improve a discriminative learner.
neurips-2006-mutagenetic-tree-fisher-ker.tldr: A kernel modeling viral evolutionary escape improves HIV drug-resistance prediction over an evolution-agnostic encoding across 17 drugs.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian methods make otherwise impractical Bayesian calculations approachable by seeking an approximate solution. However, reaching that approximation can itself be slow. This paper targets that convergence problem, proposing parameter-expanded variational Bayesian methods, abbreviated PX-VB, to accelerate the learning procedure.

The approach expands a model with auxiliary variables to reduce coupling among its original variables. It draws inspiration from parameter expansion in expectation maximization and data augmentation. The key idea is to change the representation used during computation so that the approximate inference procedure can progress more quickly toward its solution.

The authors analyze convergence rates for ordinary VB and PX-VB. They demonstrate superior convergence rates for PX-VB in variational probit regression and automatic relevance determination. These results support parameter expansion as a way to improve the speed of variational computation in the demonstrated settings. The improvement concerns how rapidly the approximation is reached; the method remains within the variational Bayesian approach to making Bayesian inference practical.
neurips-2006-parameter-expanded-variatio.tldr: Parameter expansion reduces variable coupling and accelerates variational Bayesian convergence in two demonstrated applications.

paragraphs: PG-means addresses choosing the number of clusters in a Gaussian mixture model. Instead of requiring that number to be fixed in advance, the algorithm evaluates whether the current model adequately represents the observed examples. The paper describes the resulting procedure as robust and efficient.

The method uses statistical hypothesis tests on one-dimensional projections of both the data and the model. These tests assess the mixture as a whole, rather than testing each cluster separately. This distinction makes overall model adequacy the basis for deciding whether the chosen number of clusters is sufficient to describe the examples.

The authors report good performance in difficult settings that include non-Gaussian data, overlapping clusters, elongated clusters, high-dimensional data, and many true clusters. They also find that PG-means estimates cluster counts much more stably than existing methods. The findings support using projected comparisons of the complete model to guide cluster-count selection, including in the challenging cases examined in the study.
neurips-2006-pg-means-learning-the-numbe.tldr: PG-means uses tests on one-dimensional projections to select Gaussian-mixture cluster counts more stably than the compared methods.

paragraphs: This paper designs an online algorithm for principal component analysis. On each trial, it projects the current observation onto a low-dimensional subspace chosen probabilistically. The algorithm therefore makes a sequence of randomized projection choices as observations arrive, rather than relying on a single subspace selected with access to the complete sequence.

The theoretical comparison is with the best subspace that could have been chosen in hindsight. Performance is measured by total quadratic approximation error, which evaluates the discrepancy introduced by projecting the observations. The paper relates the algorithm's expected total error to that hindsight benchmark plus an additional term.

The additional term grows linearly with the dimension of the retained subspace and logarithmically with the dimension of the original observations. This separates two distinct costs: keeping more dimensions increases the term linearly, while increasing the input dimension affects it only logarithmically. The guarantee concerns expected cumulative error for the randomized algorithm, providing a precise account of the cost of making projection decisions online.
neurips-2006-randomized-pca-algorithms-w.tldr: Randomized online PCA has an expected-error guarantee whose extra term grows only logarithmically with input dimension.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis extracts independent features from visual data, but its linear structure leaves nonlinear redundancy unaddressed. This paper asks how ICA can be applied repeatedly to capture structure beyond a single layer. The authors identify repeatability as a problem for earlier attempts to build hierarchical versions of ICA.

Their solution inserts a transformation between successive applications. It takes the absolute values of the outputs from one ICA stage and transforms them into a normal distribution. ICA can then be applied again to the transformed representation. This creates a repeatable sequence in which each stage supplies suitable input for the next.

The resulting recursive algorithm can be applied any number of times to extract higher-order structure from preceding layers. Its main contribution is therefore a simple mechanism for continuing the hierarchy, addressing the lack of a natural repeated application in prior approaches. The abstract establishes the recursive construction and its intended role in capturing residual structure, without claiming that every additional layer necessarily improves a particular task.
neurips-2006-recursive-ica-dd7588510b.tldr: Transforming the magnitudes of ICA outputs into a normal distribution enables repeated ICA layers that extract higher-order structure.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction from independent, identically distributed examples labeled by a concept in a specified class. After observing n minus one examples, a learner predicts the label of another point. Earlier one-inclusion methods bounded the worst-case error probability by VC dimension divided by n, using a graph that represents the concept class.

The first contribution tightens the graph-density bound underlying that analysis. The proof uses a new shifting operation that preserves VC dimension, together with group-theoretic symmetrization. The result resolves a conjecture concerning an unlabeled compression scheme and improves one-inclusion mistake bounds, with the deterministic improvement subject to an additional dimension condition.

The second contribution extends the approach to multiclass prediction through a hypergraph version of one-inclusion. Its bound replaces VC dimension with Pollard pseudo-dimension. The expected-risk bound improves on known PAC-based results by an O(log n) factor and is optimal up to an O(log k) factor for k classes. These are theoretical improvements connecting the combinatorial structure of a concept class to prediction guarantees.
neurips-2006-shifting-one-inclusion-mist.tldr: New combinatorial bounds improve one-inclusion prediction guarantees and extend them to multiclass learning with near-optimal expected-risk bounds.

paragraphs: Standard support vector machine training does not give users an explicit control over how many support vectors define the resulting classifier. This paper introduces a modified formulation with a user-selected budget parameter B. The aim is to give sparsity a direct role in the training formulation.

The proposed objective concentrates on the loss of the B worst-classified training examples and ignores the remaining examples in that loss calculation. The authors use this idea to derive sparse versions of both L1-SVM and L2-SVM. Technically, they replace the usual 1-norm in the standard formulation with interpolation norms that support the modified objective.

The paper also adapts the SMO optimization algorithm to solve the new formulations and reports preliminary experiments. Its contribution combines a budget-oriented learning objective with a corresponding optimization method. The central change is which training losses receive attention: the formulation explicitly focuses on the hardest B examples, providing a route to sparse classifiers within both SVM variants discussed.
neurips-2006-support-vector-machines-on-.tldr: A budget parameter focuses SVM training on the B worst-classified examples, yielding sparse formulations with an adapted optimization algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a mathematical connection between probabilistic message passing and neural network dynamics. The authors derive the equations of a continuous Hopfield network from belief propagation on a binary Markov random field. The connection provides a precise relationship between two descriptions of computation: messages exchanged in a probabilistic model and evolving activity in a neural network.

A key part of the argument concerns convergence. Hopfield networks have a Lyapunov function that supports a convergence guarantee. The authors use this property to identify a connection with belief propagation that avoids convergence problems for the relevant message initializations.

The exact implementation statement applies in the limit where each neuron has many weak connections. In that limit, Hopfield networks implement a continuous-time form of belief propagation with the specified initialization behavior. These conditions are central to the result. The contribution gives a rigorous way to understand how neural dynamics can correspond to probabilistic inference and informs the interpretation of message passing in biological neural networks.
neurips-2006-the-neurodynamics-of-belief.tldr: In the many-weak-connections limit, continuous Hopfield networks exactly implement a convergent continuous-time form of belief propagation with suitable initializations.

paragraphs: This paper learns a probabilistic object grammar from training examples without supervision. The grammar supports both object detection and parsing, so it provides a structured interpretation of an object as well as recognizing its presence. The approach is invariant to object scale and rotation.

The authors demonstrate the method on thirteen objects from Caltech 101. They also learn a hybrid class containing faces, motorbikes, and airplanes without knowing the specific object, its position, scale, or pose. The individual object types can then be recovered as different aspects of the learned grammar, showing how a shared model can represent a mixed collection.

The models are learned on training datasets and evaluated on separate test datasets, with comparisons to alternative approaches. Reported advantages include inference in under one second, object parsing, and increased accuracy. These results support the grammar as both a recognition model and a structured description of objects. The authors also present the approach as broadly applicable to other objects and structures.
neurips-2006-unsupervised-learning-of-a-.tldr: An unsupervised probabilistic grammar detects and parses objects, including mixed object classes, with reported accuracy gains and subsecond inference.
